q: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies within which country?
explain: About 60% of the Amazon rainforest is inside Brazil, the largest country in South America.

q: Which sport is Brazil's national passion? Brazil has won the men's World Cup more times than any other country.
explain: Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup five times, more than any other country.

q: Which two imaginary lines cross Brazil?
options: The Prime Meridian and the Equator
The Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
The Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn
The Equator and the Tropic of Cancer
explain: Both the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn pass through Brazil.

q: Which is the largest city in Brazil?
explain: São Paulo is Brazil's largest city and one of the biggest in the world.

q: The Pantanal, one of the world's largest tropical wetlands, is mostly in which country?
explain: The Pantanal, a vast seasonally flooded wetland, is mostly in western Brazil.

q: Capoeira, a martial art disguised as a dance, comes from which country?
explain: Capoeira was created by enslaved Africans in Brazil, mixing martial arts, music, and dance.

q: The Rio Negro, a major tributary of the Amazon, meets the Amazon River at which Brazilian city?
explain: At Manaus, the dark Rio Negro meets the sandy Amazon — the famous 'Meeting of Waters'.

q: Brazil shares borders with how many other South American countries?
explain: Brazil borders 10 of South America's 12 countries — every one except Chile and Ecuador.

q: Which drink, brewed from the yerba mate herb, is a beloved tradition in Argentina?
explain: Mate is a bitter herbal tea shared from a gourd with a metal straw — a social ritual across Argentina.

q: The Río de la Plata is a huge estuary shared by Argentina and which country?
explain: The Río de la Plata, the widest river estuary in the world, separates Argentina from Uruguay.

q: Tierra del Fuego, the island at the southern tip of South America, is shared by Argentina and which country?
explain: Tierra del Fuego, 'Land of Fire', is divided between Argentina and Chile.

q: Which Argentine city is famous for the colourful houses of La Boca and the birthplace of tango?
explain: Buenos Aires, Argentina's capital, is the home of tango and the brightly painted La Boca district.

q: Patagonia, the windswept region at the southern end of South America, is shared by Argentina and which country?
explain: Patagonia, famous for glaciers and wide open plains, spans southern Argentina and Chile.

q: Which Argentine cowboy, famous for his lasso skills and silver-ornamented gear, is a national symbol?
explain: The gaucho is the iconic horseman of the Argentine and Uruguayan pampas.

q: Argentina shares borders with Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, and which fifth country?
explain: Argentina's five neighbors are Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, and Uruguay.

q: Which Chilean poet won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971?
explain: Pablo Neruda, one of the great poets of the 20th century, won the 1971 Nobel Prize in Literature.

q: The Atacama Desert is so dry that some of its weather stations have never recorded what?
explain: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations have never recorded any rainfall.

q: Valparaíso, a colourful port city with historic funiculars, is in which country?
explain: Valparaíso, a hilly port city with brightly painted houses and old funicular lifts, is in Chile.

q: Ojos del Salado, the world's highest volcano, lies on the border of Chile and which country?
explain: Ojos del Salado, at 6,893 metres on the Chile-Argentina border, is the world's highest volcano.

q: The Juan Fernández Islands, where the sailor Alexander Selkirk was stranded, belong to which country?
explain: Chile's Juan Fernández Islands, including Robinson Crusoe Island, inspired the novel Robinson Crusoe.

q: The Atacama Desert lies between the Andes Mountains and which ocean?
explain: The Atacama, on Chile's northern coast, is squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific Ocean.

q: Which Peruvian dish of raw fish 'cooked' in lime juice is famous worldwide?
explain: Ceviche is Peru's signature dish — fresh fish marinated in lime juice with onions and chilli.

q: Which city was the capital of the Inca Empire?
explain: Cusco, high in the Andes, was the capital of the Inca Empire.

q: Which animal, used by the Incas to carry goods through the mountains, is a symbol of Peru?
explain: Llamas have carried goods across the Andes for thousands of years and are a symbol of Peru.

q: The Amazon River rises in the Andes of which country?
explain: The Amazon's source is a small stream high in the Peruvian Andes.

q: Which Peruvian city is the gateway to Machu Picchu?
explain: Travellers pass through Cusco, the old Inca capital, on the way to Machu Picchu.

q: The Ballestas Islands, home to sea lions, penguins, and huge bird colonies, are often called 'the poor man's Galápagos' — they belong to which country?
explain: Peru's Ballestas Islands are a wildlife haven just off the coast near Pisco.

q: The Nazca Lines, giant ancient drawings in the desert, are in which country?
explain: The Nazca Lines in southern Peru are huge geoglyphs best seen from the air.

q: Colombia has coastlines on which two bodies of water?
options: The Pacific Ocean and the Southern Ocean
The Caribbean Sea and the Mediterranean Sea
The Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea
The Atlantic Ocean and the Indian Ocean
explain: Colombia is one of the few South American countries with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.

q: Colombia is named after which explorer?
explain: Colombia is named after Christopher Columbus, the explorer who reached the Americas in 1492.

q: The 'Coffee Triangle' (Eje Cafetero), a famous coffee-growing region, is in which country?
explain: Colombia's Coffee Triangle, a UNESCO landscape, grows some of the world's finest coffee.

q: Which Colombian city is nicknamed 'The City of Eternal Spring' for its pleasant climate?
explain: Medellín, in the Andes, enjoys spring-like weather all year round.

q: The Magdalena River, Colombia's principal river, flows into which sea?
explain: The Magdalena River flows north through Colombia and empties into the Caribbean at Barranquilla.

q: San Andrés and Providencia, Caribbean islands with a distinct culture, belong to which country?
explain: San Andrés and Providencia are a Colombian archipelago in the western Caribbean.

q: What is the highest mountain in Colombia?
explain: Pico Cristóbal Colón, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, is Colombia's highest peak at 5,775 metres.

q: The Orinoco River, one of South America's great rivers, flows mainly through which country?
explain: The Orinoco River flows about 2,000 km, mostly through Venezuela.

q: Margarita Island, a popular Venezuelan resort island, lies in which sea?
explain: Margarita Island, in the Caribbean Sea, is one of Venezuela's favourite holiday spots.

q: Venezuela's name means 'little Venice' — explorers saw houses on stilts on which lake?
explain: Venezuela was named 'little Venice' after the stilt houses explorers saw on Lake Maracaibo.

q: What is the highest mountain in Venezuela?
explain: Pico Bolívar, in the Mérida Andes, is Venezuela's highest peak at 4,978 metres.

q: Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall, plunges from which flat-topped mountain?
explain: Angel Falls drops 979 metres from the cliffs of Auyán-tepui in Venezuela.

q: The Los Roques archipelago, a Caribbean paradise of cays and coral reefs, belongs to which country?
explain: Los Roques, a national park of islands and reefs, is a Venezuelan archipelago in the Caribbean.

q: Venezuela shares borders with Colombia, Brazil, and which third country?
explain: Venezuela's three neighbors are Colombia, Brazil, and Guyana.

q: Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, is a major port on which river?
explain: Guayaquil, Ecuador's biggest city and main port, sits on the Guayas River.

q: Cuenca, a beautiful colonial city high in the Andes, is in which country?
explain: Cuenca, Ecuador's third-largest city, is a UNESCO-listed colonial gem in the Andes.

q: Cotopaxi, one of the world's highest active volcanoes, is in which country?
explain: Cotopaxi, at 5,897 metres in Ecuador, is one of the world's highest active volcanoes.

q: The 'Avenue of the Volcanoes', a string of high peaks, is in which country?
explain: Ecuador's Avenue of the Volcanoes runs along the Andes, dotted with towering peaks.

q: Which mountain's summit is the farthest point from the Earth's centre, thanks to the equatorial bulge?
explain: Chimborazo in Ecuador is not the tallest above sea level, but its summit is the farthest from Earth's centre.

q: Bolivia is named after which South American independence leader?
explain: Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar, the liberator of much of South America.

q: The Altiplano, a vast high plateau shared with Peru, is a region of which country?
explain: Bolivia's Altiplano is a high, treeless plateau where llamas graze and people farm quinoa.

q: Which country is home to the city of Potosí, once one of the world's highest cities and a famous silver-mining boomtown?
explain: Potosí, in Bolivia, sits at about 4,090 metres and was once the world's largest silver-mining centre.

q: What is the highest peak in Bolivia?
explain: Sajama, a dormant volcano in the Andes, is Bolivia's highest peak at 6,542 metres.

q: The Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, is in which country?
explain: Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat — over 10,000 square kilometres of white salt.

q: The Salar de Uyuni sits on huge reserves of which metal used in batteries?
explain: Under the Salar de Uyuni's salt crust lie some of the world's largest lithium reserves, used in batteries.

q: Paraguay is landlocked between Bolivia, Brazil, and which third country?
explain: Paraguay's three neighbors are Brazil, Bolivia, and Argentina.

q: Which indigenous language, spoken by most Paraguayans, is an official language alongside Spanish?
explain: Guaraní, an indigenous language, is co-official in Paraguay and spoken by most of the population.

q: The Gran Chaco, a hot, semi-arid lowland, covers much of which country?
explain: The Gran Chaco, a hot plain of forests and grasslands, covers much of western Paraguay.

q: The Itaipu Dam, one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants, is shared by Paraguay and which country?
explain: The Itaipu Dam on the Paraná River is shared by Paraguay and Brazil.

q: The Jesuit missions of La Santísima Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue, UNESCO sites, are in which country?
explain: Paraguay's Jesuit missions were built by Jesuit priests and Guaraní people in the 1600s and 1700s.

q: The Paraguay River flows into which larger river?
explain: The Paraguay River is a major tributary of the Paraná River.

q: Uruguay is the second-smallest country in South America — which country is the smallest?
explain: Suriname is South America's smallest country; Uruguay is the second smallest.

q: Uruguay hosted and won the first ever FIFA World Cup — in which year?
explain: Uruguay won the first FIFA World Cup on home soil in 1930.

q: Uruguay's full name is 'República Oriental del Uruguay' — 'Oriental' means it lies east of which river?
explain: 'Oriental' refers to Uruguay's position east of the Uruguay River.

q: Punta del Este, a glamorous beach resort on the Atlantic coast, is in which country?
explain: Punta del Este is Uruguay's most famous beach resort, east of Montevideo.

q: The carnival in which Uruguayan capital is one of the longest in the world?
explain: Montevideo's carnival is famous for lasting over 40 days, one of the longest in the world.

q: The Uruguay River forms part of the border between Uruguay and which country?
explain: The Uruguay River separates Uruguay from Argentina.

q: Guyana is part of a region called the Guianas, along with Suriname and which other territory?
explain: The Guianas are Guyana, Suriname, and French Guiana, on South America's northeast coast.

q: Kaieteur Falls, one of the world's most powerful waterfalls, is in which country?
explain: Kaieteur Falls in Guyana drops 226 metres in a single leap — one of the world's tallest single-drop waterfalls.

q: Guyana borders Venezuela, Brazil, and which third country?
explain: Guyana's three neighbors are Venezuela, Brazil, and Suriname.

q: The name 'Guyana' comes from an indigenous word meaning what?
explain: Guyana comes from an Arawak word meaning 'land of many waters', for its rivers and waterfalls.

q: Kaieteur Falls is on which river in Guyana?
explain: Kaieteur Falls thunders over a cliff on the Potaro River in western Guyana.

q: Mount Roraima, a flat-topped mountain where Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil meet, inspired which famous adventure novel?
explain: Arthur Conan Doyle's 'The Lost World' was inspired by Mount Roraima in Guyana.

q: Suriname borders Guyana, Brazil, and which other territory?
explain: Suriname's three neighbors are Guyana, French Guiana, and Brazil.

q: Suriname was formerly a colony of which European country?
explain: Suriname was a Dutch colony, and Dutch is still its official language.

q: Most of Suriname is covered by which type of landscape?
explain: Tropical rainforest covers most of Suriname, one of the greenest countries on Earth.

q: Paramaribo, the capital of Suriname, is a UNESCO site on the bank of which river?
explain: Paramaribo, Suriname's capital, sits on the Suriname River.

q: Which people, descended from enslaved Africans who escaped into the interior, live in traditional villages in Suriname's rainforests?
explain: The Maroons of Suriname live in the rainforest interior, keeping African traditions alive.

q: The Drake Passage separates South America from which continent?
explain: The Drake Passage, between Cape Horn and Antarctica, is the roughest sea crossing in the world.

q: Which line of latitude passes through the northern part of South America?
explain: The Equator crosses the northern countries of South America, including Ecuador, Colombia, and Brazil.

q: The Andes Mountains pass through how many South American countries?
explain: The Andes run through seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina.

q: Which South American river has the largest drainage basin in the world?
explain: The Amazon basin drains about 7 million square kilometres — the largest of any river on Earth.
